title: Kindness to Mephibosheth
summary: David asks whether anyone is left from Saul's house to whom he can show kindness for Jonathan's sake. Saul's former servant Ziba tells him of Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, lame in both feet and living east of the Jordan. David brings him to Jerusalem, restores Saul's land to him, assigns Ziba's household to farm it, and gives Mephibosheth a permanent place at the king's table.
story: With his kingdom secure (chapter 8), David remembers a promise. Years earlier, while Saul hunted David, Jonathan had asked David to swear that he would never cut off his kindness from Jonathan's house (1 Samuel 20:14-17). Jonathan died with Saul on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31), and his five-year-old son was crippled when his nurse fell while fleeing with him at the news (2 Samuel 4:4). This chapter keeps that oath. It also opens the long section of 2 Samuel (chapters 9-20) that many scholars call the court history or succession narrative, the story of David's household and of who will sit on his throne. Mephibosheth and Ziba will return in chapters 16 and 19, when Absalom's revolt tests every loyalty.
historical:
In the ancient Near East, a man who founded a new dynasty usually removed the surviving males of the old one, since any of them could become the rallying point for a rival claim. Israel's own later history shows the pattern: Baasha wiped out the house of Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:29), and Jehu the house of Ahab (2 Kings 10). Mephibosheth had good reason to be living quietly in Lo-debar, a town in Gilead east of the Jordan, in the house of Machir son of Ammiel, and good reason to fall on his face in fear when summoned. Machir himself will later bring supplies to David when he flees Absalom (17:27-29), which suggests that David's kindness here won friends east of the Jordan.

Mephibosheth's name also has a history. In 1 Chronicles 8:34 and 9:40 he is called Merib-baal. Many scholars think the element baal (which could simply mean lord) was later replaced in Samuel with bosheth, meaning shame, because Baal was the name of the Canaanite storm god. The same change appears in the name of Saul's son Ish-bosheth, called Eshbaal in Chronicles.
cultural:
Eating at the king's table was a public honor and a form of permanent support. It could also be a way of keeping a potential rival close. The same arrangement ends the books of Kings, when the Babylonian king releases the exiled King Jehoiachin from prison and gives him a place at his table for the rest of his life (2 Kings 25:27-30). The land of Saul's family, probably around Gibeah in Benjamin, had likely passed to the crown or been managed by Ziba. David returns it to its heir and makes Ziba, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, responsible for working it.

Mephibosheth calls himself “a dead dog” (verse 8), the lowest self-description available in that culture, where dogs were scavengers rather than pets. Physical disability could also bring social shame; the saying in 5:8 about the blind and the lame shows the attitude of the time. David's welcome cuts against both his rank and his weakness.
literary: The chapter is built around a single word, kindness (chesed), which David uses three times (verses 1, 3, and 7), and around the table, mentioned four times. The phrase “eat at my table” and its variants frame the second half, and the chapter ends on a deliberately unresolved note: Mephibosheth “always ate at the king's table, and he was lame in both feet.” The last clause keeps his weakness in view even as he sits among the king's sons. The dialogue is spare, and the repeated “I am your servant” (verses 2 and 6) shows both Ziba and Mephibosheth bowing before a king whose intentions they cannot yet know.

outline.t: David seeks someone from Saul's house to show kindness
Saul's land restored, and Ziba assigned to farm it

doctrines.note: David acts on a sworn promise made to Jonathan years before. Covenant faithfulness here reaches beyond the one to whom the promise was made, to his descendant who had done nothing to earn it.

The chapter is history, not allegory, but it has long served as a picture of grace: someone from a fallen house, unable to come on his own, is sought out, spared, restored, and seated at the king's table for another's sake.

words.note: Chesed, kindness or loyal love. David speaks of “the kindness of God” (verse 3), meaning kindness of the kind God shows, or kindness sworn before God. The word implies loyalty to a relationship, here the covenant with Jonathan, carried out with generosity beyond what was required.

Shulchan, table. Mentioned four times, the table is the chapter's central image: provision, honor, and belonging. To eat at the king's table was to be treated “like one of the king's own sons” (verse 11).

Kelev, dog. In the Old Testament dogs are scavengers, and calling oneself a dog, especially a dead one, is extreme self-abasement. Mephibosheth expects nothing; the gap between his words and David's gift is the point.

Mephibosheth, the name of Jonathan's son. His alternate name in Chronicles, Merib-baal, suggests that the -bosheth (shame) ending was a later substitution for baal. The name is a reminder that baal, meaning lord or master, was once an ordinary element in Israelite names, before its association with the Canaanite god led later scribes to avoid it.

christ: The New Testament does not quote this chapter, and it should not be read as a coded prophecy. Its link to Christ is one of pattern. Jesus, the greater son of David, describes the kingdom of God as a banquet to which the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame are brought in (Luke 14:12-24), and he eats with those others considered unworthy. Christians have seen in David's kindness to Mephibosheth a small, true picture of the grace that seeks out the helpless for another's sake and gives them a permanent place at the king's table. The Lord's Supper, and the hope of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9), carry that image forward.

hard.q: Was David's kindness genuine, or was he keeping a possible rival under watch?
hard.a: Some interpreters read the chapter with political suspicion. Mephibosheth was Saul's heir, and bringing him to Jerusalem kept him within reach; some have also argued that chapter 21, where David hands over seven of Saul's descendants for execution, took place before this chapter, so that David's question in verse 1 is less innocent than it sounds. Others take the narrator at his word: David is keeping an oath to Jonathan, and he restores property that he could easily have kept. Both things can be true at once, since in the ancient world generosity and prudence often walked together. The text itself frames the act in terms of chesed and Jonathan, and it records that David later spared Mephibosheth for the sake of that oath (21:7).

questions: David remembered a promise made years earlier, when he was in danger and Jonathan was powerful. What promises have you made that are easy to forget now that circumstances have changed?
Mephibosheth saw himself as a dead dog. How does being welcomed despite what you think of yourself change the way you live?
The chapter ends by noting that he was still lame. What does it mean that grace gave him a seat at the table without first removing his weakness?
